beginner: Bell peppers like rich, well-drained soil that warms up in the sun, since they are warm-season plants that dislike cold, soggy ground. Mix in 2 to 3 inches of compost before planting. If your soil is heavy clay or slow to warm, a sheet of black plastic or fabric mulch laid down before planting warms the soil and gives peppers the head start they want. Aim for soil that stays evenly moist but never waterlogged, because uneven watering is what causes the dark, sunken blossom-end rot on the bottom of the fruit.
seasoned: Bell pepper wants a deep, fertile, well-drained loam or sandy loam rich in organic matter, and a soil that warms early and holds steady moisture. As a warm-season crop it sulks in cold, wet ground, so a sandy loam that warms quickly in spring suits it better than a heavy, slow-warming clay. Work 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before planting, and on heavy or cool soils many growers lay black plastic or fabric mulch to raise soil temperature and set transplants into warmer ground. Even soil moisture in a freely draining bed is the target, because the wide swings between dry and soaked that a poorly drained soil produces are the direct cause of the calcium-starved blossom-end rot bell peppers are prone to.

beginner: Bell peppers like slightly acidic soil, about pH 6.0 to 6.8, and a lot of garden soil is already close. The pH scale runs from acidic to alkaline, and this range is where peppers take up nutrients best, including the calcium that prevents blossom-end rot. If your soil runs alkaline, common in the dry interior West, you may need to add sulfur before planting. An inexpensive soil test from your local extension office tells you where you stand.
seasoned: Bell pepper grows best at a soil pH of about 6.0 to 6.8, with Clemson placing the sweet spot near 6.0 to 6.5 and Minnesota noting peppers do well up to about 7.0. In that band the nutrients peppers need, including the calcium that guards against blossom-end rot, stay most available. Peppers tolerate a somewhat wider range, roughly 5.5 to 7.5, but uptake of iron, manganese, and other micronutrients tightens as the soil turns alkaline, showing as yellowing between the veins of the youngest leaves. Alkaline soils common across the interior West often need sulfur worked in ahead of planting; most Eastern and Midwestern soils sit naturally near the target. A soil test from your local extension office settles it before you plant.

beginner: Bell peppers like steady but modest feeding, and going heavy on nitrogen backfires. Mix a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again once the first peppers set, feed with a nitrogen fertilizer like calcium nitrate. Do not overdo it: too much nitrogen gives you a large leafy plant with few peppers. Calcium nitrate also supplies calcium, which, along with even watering, helps prevent blossom-end rot.
seasoned: Bell pepper is a moderate feeder that rewards restraint with nitrogen. Work a balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10, or 2 to 3 pounds of it per 100 square feet, into the bed before transplanting, then side-dress with a nitrogen source such as calcium nitrate about three to four weeks after transplanting and again as the first fruits set. Hold nitrogen back early and never overdo it: too much drives a big, bushy, dark-green plant that flowers late and sets little fruit. The calcium nitrate side-dress does double duty, feeding the plant while supplying the calcium that, paired with even watering, heads off blossom-end rot.

beginner: Your bell pepper is setting fruit. Feed it now with a nitrogen fertilizer such as calcium nitrate to keep it producing and to help prevent blossom-end rot.
seasoned: Your bell pepper is setting its first fruit, a good time to side-dress with a calcium nitrate source to feed the plant and supply calcium against blossom-end rot.

beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer like 5-10-10 at planting, then a nitrogen feed such as calcium nitrate once the plant is growing well and setting fruit. Do not overdo the nitrogen or you get all leaves and few peppers.
seasoned: A balanced fertilizer such as 5-10-10 worked in at planting, then a calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) side-dress three to four weeks after transplanting and again at fruit set. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which gives leaf at the expense of fruit.

beginner: Mix 2 to 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet (or a few inches of compost) into the soil before planting. Then, a few weeks after planting and again at fruit set, scratch a small amount of calcium nitrate into the soil a few inches out from each plant and water it in.
seasoned: A common rate is 2 to 3 pounds of 5-10-10 per 100 square feet worked into the bed before transplanting. For the side-dress, Clemson suggests about 5 pounds of calcium nitrate (15.5-0-0) per 1000 square feet or 300 feet of row, applied three to four weeks after transplanting and repeated three to four weeks later, placed a few inches out from the plants and watered in.

beginner: The most useful pepper companions are strong-smelling herbs and flowers like basil, marigold, and nasturtium, which can help deter or lure away aphids and other pests. The one rule that really matters is to keep peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which are all close relatives and share the same pests and soil diseases.
seasoned: Most pepper companion pairings are traditional rather than trial-tested. The aromatic-herb and flower companions (basil, marigold, nasturtium, alliums) are grown to deter or trap the aphids and thrips that trouble peppers and to draw beneficial insects, a plausible, habitat-based effect rather than an isolated one. The single firmest rule is a rotation one: keep peppers away from their Solanaceae relatives, tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant, which share the full pepper pest and disease complex.

beginner: Basil is a classic pepper neighbor. Its strong scent is thought to help confuse soft-bodied pests like aphids and thrips, and it tucks neatly between young pepper plants. A pleasant, low-risk companion.
seasoned: A traditional interplanting with peppers; the aromatic foliage is thought to deter aphids and thrips and to draw pollinators and beneficial insects. The effect is habitat-based and traditional rather than trial-isolated for pepper.

beginner: Marigolds are a classic companion flower for peppers, grown to help keep pests down. Mostly tradition, but cheerful and low-risk.
seasoned: A long-standing companion tradition near peppers; French marigold grown as a cover crop has documented nematode-suppressive effects, though the interplanted marigold-pepper pest benefit is traditional rather than trial-isolated.

beginner: Nasturtiums are often planted near peppers to lure aphids away from the crop. A helpful, low-risk neighbor.
seasoned: Planted as a trap and deterrent for aphids, drawing them off the peppers. Trap cropping is a documented principle, though the specific nasturtium-pepper effect is not formally isolated, so treat it as a plausible aid.

beginner: Onions, garlic, and chives have a strong smell that gardeners traditionally use to confuse pests around peppers, and they take up little room. A low-risk, space-saving neighbor.
seasoned: Pungent alliums are a traditional interplant said to mask the crop and deter soft-bodied pests; the effect is habitat-based and traditional rather than trial-isolated for pepper.

beginner: Keep peppers away from tomatoes, potatoes, and eggplant. They are all close relatives that share the same soil diseases and pests, so planting them together makes those problems worse.
seasoned: All are Solanaceae and share pepper's pest and disease complex, including bacterial leaf spot, the mosaic viruses, Phytophthora blight, anthracnose, and aphids. Grouping them concentrates that pressure and lets soilborne problems build. A real epidemiology and rotation principle rather than a tested adjacency effect: spread the nightshades out and rotate them on at least a 3 year cycle.

beginner: Many gardeners keep fennel away from peppers and most other vegetables, since it is said to stunt their growth. This is more tradition than a proven rule.
seasoned: A widely repeated caution that fennel inhibits the growth of many garden vegetables and is best kept to its own corner. There is no strong T1 mechanism for a pepper-fennel antagonism, so it persists mostly as garden lore.

beginner: Tiny soft green insects gather on new growth and the undersides of leaves, making them curl and yellow, often with a sticky film and black mold. They can also spread plant viruses to peppers.
seasoned: Colonies of small soft-bodied insects, most often green peach aphid, cluster on growing tips and the undersides of leaves, curling and yellowing the foliage, with sticky honeydew and sooty mold following. Beyond direct feeding, aphids transmit the mosaic viruses that mottle and distort pepper leaves, which is their most serious effect on the crop.

beginner: Small sap-sucking insects that multiply quickly in warm weather, especially on soft, over-fertilized growth. They also carry viruses from plant to plant.
seasoned: Several aphid species, predominantly green peach aphid, that suck sap and reproduce rapidly in warm weather, building up fast on the soft growth that excess nitrogen produces. As virus carriers they matter out of proportion to the feeding damage they do.

beginner: Blast them off with a strong spray of water and treat the undersides of the leaves with insecticidal soap, repeating every few days. Ladybugs and other helpful insects eat aphids, so welcome them.
seasoned: Knock colonies off with a strong jet of water and spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil with thorough coverage of the leaf undersides, repeating every few days. Conserve ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps, which usually bring aphids under control.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen, check the undersides of leaves regularly, and let helpful insects do their work. A silver reflective mulch under young plants helps keep aphids off.
seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which drives the soft growth aphids favor, scout leaf undersides and growing tips, and support natural enemies rather than spraying broadly. Reflective mulch deters aphids from young plants and slows virus spread.

beginner: The leaves are peppered with lots of tiny round holes, as if hit by birdshot. It hits young plants hardest. Touch the plant and you will see tiny dark beetles jump away.
seasoned: Tiny shot-hole punctures riddle the leaves, a scatter of small round holes that is the classic flea-beetle signature. Damage is worst on seedlings and young transplants, whose small leaf area a heavy infestation can shred; established peppers tolerate considerable feeding. Brush a plant and the small dark beetles spring away like fleas.

beginner: Small dark beetles that jump like fleas and chew tiny holes in the leaves. They are most active in spring and target young plants early in the season.
seasoned: Several flea beetle species that feed on pepper foliage, overwintering as adults in debris and emerging to attack the earliest, most vulnerable plants in spring. Young transplants are far more at risk than large, established plants.

beginner: Cover young plants with a light row cover until they are big and strong, then take it off when they flower. Setting out larger transplants helps them outgrow the damage. For heavy attacks, an organic spray such as spinosad helps.
seasoned: Protect transplants with floating row cover until they are large and vigorous, removing it at flowering so pollinators can reach the blooms. Set out stout, well-hardened transplants so plants can outgrow the damage, and treat heavy early infestations with spinosad or kaolin clay.

beginner: Cover plants early with row cover, set out larger transplants into warm soil so they grow quickly, and clear away weeds and old plant debris where the beetles hide over winter.
seasoned: Use row cover from transplanting, delay setting plants out until soil and air are warm so they grow away fast, and clean up crop debris and weeds that harbor overwintering adults.

beginner: Some peppers turn red too early and rot from the inside, and cutting one open reveals a small white maggot tunneling through the flesh. It is mainly a problem in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.
seasoned: Fruit that colors up early and unevenly, sometimes with a soft, rotting spot and a pinhole scar on the skin, and a white, legless maggot tunneling in the flesh inside. Cut the pepper open and the winding feeding channels and the maggot give it away. It is a regional pest, most troublesome in the Northeast and Mid-Atlantic.

beginner: A fly that lays its eggs in young peppers in summer; the maggot that hatches feeds inside the fruit, causing early ripening and rot. It is worst where the pest is established locally.
seasoned: The larva of the pepper maggot fly, which lays eggs in developing fruit through mid to late summer, leaving a tiny egg-puncture scar. The maggot feeds inside, and infested fruit ripens prematurely and often rots.

beginner: You cannot save an infested pepper, so pick off and destroy any that ripen early or show a pinhole scar to stop the next generation. Removing wild host weeds like horsenettle nearby helps.
seasoned: There is no rescue for an infested fruit, so control targets the egg-laying flies: remove and destroy affected peppers promptly to break the cycle, and where pressure is high time labeled sprays to the egg-laying period. A yellow sticky trap helps confirm when the flies are active.

beginner: Clear away wild nightshade weeds nearby, move peppers to a new spot each year, and destroy any infested fruit. In areas where it is a known problem, a floating row cover put on before fruit forms keeps the flies out.
seasoned: Remove nearby wild solanaceous weeds such as horsenettle that host the fly, rotate peppers away from last year's bed, clean up and destroy infested fruit, and in problem areas protect fruit with a labeled spray timed to the flight or with row cover before fruit set.

beginner: Whole leaves vanish, leaving just the veins, with dark droppings on the leaves below. The cause is a large green caterpillar that hides against the stems, easier to spot by its droppings than by sight.
seasoned: Large sections of leaf, and sometimes whole shoots, are stripped down to the veins, with dark pellet droppings on the leaves below. The culprits are big green tomato or tobacco hornworms, up to four inches long, that blend into the stems and are easiest to find by their frass.

beginner: Big green caterpillars, the young of large moths, that feed on pepper leaves and fruit mostly in mid to late summer. Even a few can strip a lot of foliage.
seasoned: Tomato and tobacco hornworms, the larvae of large sphinx moths, which feed on solanaceous foliage including pepper from midsummer on. A few caterpillars can do conspicuous damage given their size, and they will chew into fruit as well as leaves.

beginner: Pick the caterpillars off by hand and drop them in soapy water. If you find one covered in small white capsules, leave it, those are parasitic wasps that will do the work for you. An organic Bt spray works on the smaller caterpillars.
seasoned: Hand-pick the caterpillars, which is effective in a home garden, and apply Bacillus thuringiensis to younger larvae where numbers are high. Leave any hornworm studded with white parasitic-wasp cocoons in place, since the wasps will kill it and breed more.

beginner: Turn the soil at the end of the season to destroy the pupae, watch for droppings and missing leaves from midsummer, and welcome the helpful wasps that attack hornworms.
seasoned: Till the soil in fall to destroy overwintering pupae, scout for frass and stripped leaves from midsummer, and encourage the parasitic wasps and other natural enemies that keep hornworms in check.

beginner: Flower buds and little peppers drop off the plant, and peppers that hold on are black and rotten inside. A tiny dark, long-nosed beetle is the cause. It is mainly a problem in the warm South.
seasoned: Buds and small fruit drop from the plant, and cut-open fruit is black and frass-filled inside, its core rotted where a grub has fed. The dark, long-snouted adult weevil, about an eighth of an inch, feeds on buds and leaves. It is a serious pest of the warm South and, once established, is very hard to shake.

beginner: A small weevil whose grubs develop inside pepper buds and fruit, causing them to drop and rot. It builds up quickly in warm weather and survives on leftover pepper plants and weeds.
seasoned: Anthonomus eugenii, a small weevil whose larvae develop inside pepper buds and fruit. Adults feed on foliage and lay eggs in buds and young fruit, causing them to drop; multiple overlapping generations build fast in warm climates, and the pest overwinters on volunteer peppers and nightshade weeds.

beginner: You cannot save infested peppers, so gather and destroy every dropped bud and fruit to stop the next generation, and pull up old pepper plants and nearby nightshade weeds at season's end. Keeping the area clean is the main defense.
seasoned: There is no home-garden cure for infested fruit, so sanitation is central: pick up and destroy all dropped buds and fruit promptly to break the breeding cycle, remove volunteer peppers and nightshade weeds, and end the season by pulling and destroying spent plants. Where established, labeled sprays are timed to the adults.

beginner: Buy healthy transplants, keep the garden free of leftover pepper plants and nightshade weeds, clean up dropped buds and fruit, and do not plant peppers in the same spot as last year.
seasoned: Start with clean transplants (the weevil moves on infested plants), remove volunteer peppers and solanaceous weeds that harbor it, destroy dropped fruit through the season, and rotate away from last year's pepper ground.

beginner: Little holes near the top of the pepper, sometimes with sawdust-like droppings, and a caterpillar tunneling inside that makes the fruit rot. It is common where field corn is grown.
seasoned: Small entry holes near the stem-end cap of the fruit, often with crumbly frass, and a caterpillar tunneling inside that leads to premature ripening and rot. The borer also tunnels stems, which can wilt or break. It is a common pepper pest in the corn-growing Midwest and East.

beginner: A caterpillar, the young of a moth, that bores into peppers near the cap and into the stems, causing rot and breakage. It has more than one generation each summer.
seasoned: The larva of the European corn borer moth, which lays eggs on peppers (and corn) in summer; the caterpillar bores into fruit through the cap and into stems. Two or more generations a season are common in the Midwest and East.

beginner: Catch it early: an organic Bt or spinosad spray works on the young caterpillars before they tunnel in, but does nothing once they are inside a pepper. Pick off and destroy any bored fruit.
seasoned: Scout for eggs and early larvae and apply Bacillus thuringiensis or spinosad to young caterpillars before they bore into the fruit, since once inside they are protected. Remove and destroy infested fruit, and clean up crop and nearby corn debris at season's end.

beginner: Clean up old pepper and corn stalks at the end of the season, watch for the caterpillars from midsummer, and treat while they are small. Cleaning up where they overwinter is the biggest help.
seasoned: Destroy crop debris and nearby cornstalks where the borer overwinters, scout from midsummer when moths are flying, and time treatment to newly hatched larvae. Choosing an earlier variety can dodge the worst of the flight in some areas.

beginner: Small dark, water-soaked spots on the leaves that spread and turn brown or black, often ringed in yellow, with rough scabby spots on the peppers too. Bad cases drop leaves and expose the fruit to sunburn. It thrives in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Small, water-soaked spots on the leaves that turn brown to black with a slightly raised, scabby center and a yellow halo; badly spotted leaves yellow and drop, and raised, cracked, scabby lesions form on the fruit. Defoliation exposes the remaining fruit to sunscald. It is one of the most common and damaging pepper diseases, worst in warm, wet, splashy weather.

beginner: A bacterial disease carried on seed and in old plant debris that spreads in splashing water during warm, wet weather. It often comes in on infected seed or transplants.
seasoned: Xanthomonas bacteria that are both seedborne and carried on crop debris, spreading in splashing water and on hands and tools. Warm, humid, rainy conditions favor it, and infected seed or transplants often start an outbreak, so clean seed and rotation are central to control.

beginner: There is no cure, so pull off badly spotted leaves and avoid handling the plants when they are wet. A copper spray can slow it down but will not cure it, so prevention matters most.
seasoned: There is no cure once plants are infected; remove the worst-affected leaves and avoid working among wet plants. Copper-based sprays can slow spread but do not eradicate it, so the emphasis is on preventing it in the first place.

beginner: Use clean seed and healthy transplants, look for resistant varieties, do not plant peppers in the same spot for a few years, mulch the soil, water at the base instead of over the leaves, and clean up old plants in fall.
seasoned: Start with certified disease-free or hot-water-treated seed and clean transplants, choose resistant varieties where available, rotate peppers out of the bed for two to three years, mulch to limit soil splash, water at the base rather than overhead, and remove crop debris at season's end.

beginner: The plant wilts and collapses suddenly, often with a dark rotten patch on the stem near the soil, and the roots and even the fruit can rot. It strikes in warm, wet, soggy ground and moves fast. It is one of the worst pepper diseases.
seasoned: Dark, water-soaked lesions girdle the stem at or near the soil line and the plant wilts and collapses suddenly, sometimes with a white cottony growth; roots rot, and fruit can develop a firm, white-mold rot. It flares in warm, wet, poorly drained ground and after heavy rain or flooding, and is the most serious pepper disease in much of the country.

beginner: A mold-like disease that lives in wet soil and spreads in splashing and running water, attacking peppers in warm, soggy conditions. It moves fast once it starts and lives in the soil for years.
seasoned: Phytophthora capsici, a water mold that thrives in saturated soil and spreads in splashing and running water. It survives in soil and debris for years and moves fast in warm, wet weather, especially on heavy or poorly drained ground and in low spots that stay wet.

beginner: Pull and destroy affected plants and fruit, and fix the drainage. There is no good home cure once it takes hold, so prevention is what matters.
seasoned: Remove and destroy affected plants and fruit promptly, and improve drainage immediately. There is no effective home-garden cure once plants collapse, so control is preventive and drainage-based.

beginner: Plant on raised beds or mounds so water drains away, avoid wet low spots, water at the soil and do not overwater, and rotate away from peppers for several years. Keeping the ground from staying soggy is the key.
seasoned: Plant on raised, well-drained beds or hills, avoid low spots that stay wet, water at the soil rather than overhead, do not overwater, mulch to limit splash, rotate away from peppers and other susceptible crops for at least three to four years, and keep fruit up off saturated soil.

beginner: Sunken round spots on the peppers, often with rings of tiny dark or pinkish specks, that spread into a soft rot. It is worst on ripening red peppers in warm, wet weather.
seasoned: Sunken, circular lesions on the fruit that enlarge and develop concentric rings of small dark or salmon-colored spore masses, rotting the pepper; it hits ripening and colored fruit hardest. Warm, wet, humid weather drives it, and it can ruin a fall crop of red peppers left on the plant to color.

beginner: A fungus carried on seed and in old plant debris that spreads in splashing water during warm, wet weather. Ripening peppers left on the plant are hit hardest.
seasoned: Colletotrichum fungi that are seedborne and survive on crop debris, spreading in splashing water. Warm, humid, rainy conditions favor it, and fruit left to ripen fully on the plant in such weather is especially vulnerable.

beginner: Pick off and throw away infected peppers right away, and keep the plants dry by watering at the soil. A labeled fungicide can protect the healthy fruit, but rotten ones cannot be saved.
seasoned: Remove and destroy infected fruit promptly to limit spread, and keep foliage and fruit as dry as possible. Where the disease is active a labeled fungicide can help protect healthy fruit, but rotted peppers cannot be saved.

beginner: Use clean seed, do not plant peppers in the same spot for a few years, water at the base, give plants room for air to move, pick ripe peppers promptly, and clean up old plants at the end of the season.
seasoned: Start with clean, disease-free seed, rotate peppers out of the bed for two to three years, water at the soil rather than overhead, mulch to limit splash, space for airflow, harvest ripe fruit promptly rather than letting it sit in wet weather, and remove crop debris at season's end.

beginner: Leaves turn mottled light and dark green, crinkled or misshapen, and the plant is stunted with fewer, deformed peppers. Several viruses cause this, spread mostly by aphids and thrips. There is no cure once a plant has it.
seasoned: Leaves are mottled light and dark green, often puckered, narrowed, or distorted, and the plant is stunted with reduced, sometimes bumpy or ringspotted fruit. Several viruses, including cucumber mosaic, tobacco mosaic, and tomato spotted wilt, affect peppers, spread mainly by aphids and thrips or by handling. Symptoms are permanent, since there is no cure.

beginner: Plant viruses spread mostly by aphids and thrips, and some by touch. They cannot be cured, so they are managed by keeping the carriers down and removing infected plants.
seasoned: A group of viruses (including cucumber mosaic, tobacco mosaic, and tomato spotted wilt) transmitted mainly by aphids and thrips, and some, like tobacco mosaic, also by handling and on tools. They overwinter in weeds and perennials and are moved into the crop by their insect carriers.

beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy any plant that shows mosaic symptoms so it does not spread to others, and wash your hands and tools. Keeping aphids and thrips down is the best defense.
seasoned: There is no cure; remove and destroy infected plants promptly so they do not serve as a virus reservoir, and wash hands and tools after handling them. Managing the aphids and thrips that spread the viruses is the real lever, along with controlling weed hosts.

beginner: Look for resistant varieties, keep aphids, thrips, and weeds under control, do not handle plants right after using tobacco, and pull out infected plants as soon as you spot them.
seasoned: Choose resistant varieties where available (many peppers carry virus resistance), control aphids and thrips, keep weeds down around the garden, avoid handling plants after tobacco use (tobacco mosaic), use reflective mulch to repel aphids, and remove infected plants early.

beginner: The plant wilts and dies suddenly, and at the base of the stem you find white fuzzy threads and tiny tan balls like mustard seeds. It happens in hot weather and is mainly a problem in the warm, humid South.
seasoned: A sudden wilt with a brown, rotting lesion girdling the stem right at the soil line, where a fan of white fungal threads and small tan, mustard-seed-sized resting bodies appear. The plant collapses and dies. It strikes in hot weather on many crops and is most damaging in the warm, humid South.

beginner: A soil fungus that attacks the base of the stem in hot weather. It lives in the soil for years and affects many kinds of plants, so it builds up where susceptible crops are grown repeatedly.
seasoned: Sclerotium rolfsii, a soilborne fungus with a very wide host range that survives in soil for years as tough resting bodies. It is favored by hot weather and high soil moisture, and by crop debris and mulch in contact with the stem.

beginner: There is no cure, so pull and destroy any plant that collapses from it, taking some of the soil around the base with it. Prevention is the real answer for next season.
seasoned: There is no cure for an infected plant; remove and destroy it along with the soil immediately around the stem to carry off the resting bodies. Because it persists in soil, management is preventive.

beginner: Rotate your crops, clean up or bury old plant debris, keep heavy mulch from piling against the stems, and improve drainage. In beds where it keeps appearing, solarizing the soil in summer helps.
seasoned: Rotate away from susceptible crops on a long cycle, bury crop debris deeply or remove it, keep mulch and soil pulled back from direct contact with the stem, improve drainage, and in problem beds deep plowing or soil solarization lowers the fungus.

beginner: Give peppers a steady 1 to 2 inches of water a week, more when it is hot and dry. The most important thing is to keep it even. Letting the soil go bone-dry and then soaking it is what causes the dark, sunken rot on the bottom of the peppers.
seasoned: Aim for a steady 1 to 2 inches of water per week from rain plus irrigation, more in heat or on sandy soil, delivered deeply and evenly rather than in erratic bursts. Consistency matters more for peppers than sheer quantity: the wide swings between dry and soaked that irregular watering produces are the direct cause of blossom-end rot on the fruit.

beginner: About 1 to 2 inches of water a week, soaking the soil down at least 6 inches so the roots grow deep. Keep it even and steady, especially while the plant is flowering and setting peppers, since uneven water causes blossom-end rot and dropped flowers.
seasoned: Around 1 to 2 inches per week is the working range, wetting the soil to a depth of at least 6 inches so roots follow the moisture down, and leaning higher through flowering and fruit sizing. Even, deep watering is what prevents blossom-end rot and dropped blossoms; a thorough soak once or twice a week beats a light daily sprinkle.

beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves, with a soaker hose or by holding the hose at the base. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent disease. If you must use a sprinkler, do it in the morning so the leaves dry by evening. Mulch is a big help: it keeps the soil evenly moist, which is the best way to prevent blossom-end rot.
seasoned: Water at the base with a soaker hose or drip line, keeping the foliage as dry as possible, since wet leaves favor the bacterial leaf spot and anthracnose peppers are prone to. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so leaves dry before evening. A layer of mulch buffers soil moisture, the single most useful habit for preventing blossom-end rot, and blocks soilborne spores from splashing onto the lower leaves and fruit.

beginner: If the lower leaves yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the stem goes soft near the base, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly. Soggy soil invites root and stem rots.
seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft, rotting stems point to overwatering or poor drainage. Saturated soil starves the roots of oxygen and invites the Phytophthora blight peppers are highly susceptible to, especially on heavy ground and in low, wet spots.

beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry. The clearest sign of uneven watering is blossom-end rot, a dark sunken patch on the bottom of the pepper, which comes from the soil drying out and flooding rather than from a lack of fertilizer.
seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers by evening is common in heat and not alarming, but leaves that stay limp signal real drought. The clearest sign of uneven watering is blossom-end rot: a dark, sunken, leathery patch on the blossom end of the fruit, caused not by a soil calcium shortage as such but by the plant's inability to move calcium to the fruit when moisture swings. Drought during flowering also drops blossoms and gives small fruit.

beginner: Keep the seed tray evenly damp and warm while the peppers come up. They sprout slowly, so do not let the surface dry out.
seasoned: Keep the seed-starting mix evenly moist and warm through germination; pepper seed is slow and must not dry mid-emergence.

beginner: Keep the young plants evenly damp, not soggy. Let the top of the mix begin to dry before watering again.
seasoned: Grow seedlings on under lights with even, moderate moisture, letting the surface approach dryness between waterings to keep damping off out of the tray.

beginner: Soak the plant in well when you set it out, then keep the soil evenly moist as it takes hold. A layer of mulch helps hold that moisture steady.
seasoned: Water in thoroughly at transplant to settle the roots, then hold steady, even moisture at the base as the plant establishes; mulch now to start buffering soil moisture.

beginner: Keep watering steady and even once flowers open. Uneven water now drops the flowers and starts blossom-end rot, the dark sunken patch on the bottom of the peppers. Mulch helps hold the moisture.
seasoned: Even moisture from flowering through fruit set is the first critical window: steady water sets fruit and prevents blossom drop, while dry-to-saturated swings start the blossom-end rot that peppers are so prone to. Keep it even, mulched, and deep to at least 6 inches.

beginner: Move peppers to a different part of the garden each year, and do not return them, or their relatives tomato, potato, and eggplant, to the same spot for about three years, longer if you have had Phytophthora blight. seasoned: Rotate peppers on at least a 3 year cycle, longer where Phytophthora blight has appeared, to break the buildup of bacterial leaf spot, Phytophthora, anthracnose, and southern blight in the soil. Clear and remove spent plants at season's end rather than tilling them in, which removes overwintering disease and pest sites, including the dropped fruit that harbors pepper weevil and pepper maggot.

beginner: Bell peppers keep at room temperature for a few days if kept out of the sun. For anything longer than that, put them in the fridge. Red, orange, and yellow ripe peppers do not last quite as long as green ones, so use them first.
seasoned: Bell peppers keep at room temperature for several days out of direct sun, staying firm and glossy longer than most summer fruit. For a short hold a cool spot on the counter is fine; for longer than a few days the refrigerator is better. Colored ripe peppers are more perishable than green ones and are best used sooner.

beginner: Keep peppers in the crisper drawer, loosely bagged, and they last one to two weeks. Do not store them in the coldest part of the fridge, since peppers can get pitted and soft if kept too cold. Put them away dry, not wet, so they do not rot.
seasoned: Store peppers in the crisper at about 45 to 50°F with high humidity, loosely bagged, for one to two weeks. Peppers are mildly chilling-sensitive: held below about 40°F for long they develop surface pitting and softening, so the crisper rather than the coldest part of the refrigerator is the right spot. Store them dry, since surface moisture speeds decay.

beginner: Peppers are one of the easiest vegetables to freeze, and you do not even need to blanch them first. Just wash, remove the seeds, chop them up, freeze on a tray, then pour into a bag. They keep for months and are great for cooking, though they go soft once thawed so they are not for salads.
seasoned: Bell peppers freeze unusually well and, unlike most vegetables, do not need blanching first. Simply wash, core, chop or slice, spread on a tray to freeze, then bag; they keep their flavor for many months and go straight into cooked dishes. The texture softens on thawing, so frozen peppers are for cooking, not fresh eating.

beginner: Peppers store better than many summer vegetables. Keep them cool but not cold, around 45 to 50°F, loosely bagged and dry, for one to two weeks. seasoned: Peppers are a fair keeper compared with softer summer crops. Hold them at about 45 to 50°F and high humidity, loosely bagged and dry, for one to two weeks; avoid deep cold, which causes chilling pitting. For long storage, freezing (no blanching needed) is the standout method, and peppers also dry and can well. Handle colored ripe fruit gently and use it before green fruit.

seasoned: Choose by color, season, and space. For the classic blocky bell, grow California Wonder or Big Bertha and let it ripen from green to red, or pick green for firm walls. Where the season is short or cool, early types like King of the North set and ripen fruit far more reliably. For containers and small spaces, the compact Redskin and the small snacking bells are the safest choices. Many modern hybrids also carry resistance to bacterial leaf spot and the mosaic viruses, worth seeking where those are a problem.
